segments.head: /* @module wclm/operators/tokenise
segments.label: the module's claim
segments.does: States the operator's single responsibility: words become content-hash tokens, no registry anywhere — the hash IS the identity, in this document and every other.

segments.head: 'use strict';
segments.label: strict mode + the one dependency
segments.does: Pulls fnv64 from the shared engine helpers. Nothing else is imported: the operator's whole world is the text it is given.

vars.fnv64: FNV-1a 64-bit over code points, cut to 12 hex — the shared hash both Python and JS pin

segments.head: const WORD_RE = /[A-Za-z0-9_]+(?:['’-][A-Za-z0-9_]+)*/g;
segments.label: what counts as a word
segments.does: The word rule as one regex: letters, digits, underscore, with apostrophes and hyphens allowed INSIDE a word. Changing this changes every downstream hash — deliberately boring.

vars.WORD_RE: the tokeniser's entire opinion about word boundaries

segments.head: export const block = {
segments.label: the pipeline contract
segments.does: Declares the operator to the registry: key, display name, core (cannot be toggled off), the typed io (reads text, writes tokens) the runner enforces, and the one-line role every UI shows.
writes: the registry entry the engine imports

segments.head: run(s) {
segments.label: the transformation
segments.does: Matches every word, lowercases it, and hashes the lowercase form — so Graph, GRAPH and graph are one token. Each token keeps its position i and original spelling w. The phrase then gets the hash of all token hashes joined with '+': order matters, so 'graph of graphs' and 'graphs of graphs' can never collide.

vars.s.tokens: [{i, w, form, hash}] — position, spelling, lowercase form, content address
vars.s.phrase: {text, hash} — the whole prompt's own address
